query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing trace single-atom Pt via atomic layer deposition onto the catalyst surface will create isolated noble metal sites that enhance low-temperature CO/hydrocarbon oxidation and improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning without significantly increasing overall PGM usage.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with an unmodified surface.
generation.intervention: Utilize atomic layer deposition to deposit approximately 1 wt% (or lower) of Pt as isolated single atoms dispersed across the catalyst surface.
generation.conditions: Evaluate under automotive exhaust conditions with transient low-temperature (below 150 °C) operation in the presence of typical poisons (water vapor at ≈10 vol% and NO), along with aging protocols simulating lifetime mileage (≥500 h).
generation.structural_mediator: The single-atom Pt sites, stabilized by the high-entropy substrate, modify the electronic environment to facilitate oxygen activation and reduce the binding strength of poisoning species.
generation.mechanism: The synergistic interaction between the minimal Pt sites and the base high-entropy alloy promotes a Mars–van Krevelen–type mechanism, lowering activation barriers for oxidation while mitigating CO and pollutant poisoning effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, this doped version is expected to lower the oxidation onset temperature by approximately 15–25 °C and sustain catalytic performance over extended durability tests with minimal deactivation under poisoning conditions.
generation.baseline: The original multi-principal-element alloy catalyst without noble metal doping, which, while PGM-lean, has higher oxidation temperatures and greater sensitivity to poisoning.
generation.boundary: The improvements must be observed under exhaust testing conditions representative of real-driving emissions over extended operation times.
generation.uncertainty: Potential issues include the long-term stability of single-atom dispersion under high thermal and redox cycling, and the precise dosage required to balance performance without overusing PGM.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSupported ultrafine noble metal species, especially for Pt, suffer from inevitable sintering at temperatures as low as 80 °C, severely limiting their stability and thus their practical applications. In this work, a strategy is demonstrated using the high‐entropy effect to prevent sub‐2.6 nm Pt nanoparticles from sintering. Due to the higher mixing entropy and thus lower Gibbs free energy of porous high‐entropy oxide (HEO) nanofibers in the catalytic system, the supported Pt remained thermally stable up to 1000 °C, as verified by in situ HAADF−STEM observation. Even after being hydrothermally aged with 10 vol% vapor at 850 °C, this catalytic system maintained the Pt size of 2.9 nm, demonstrating remarkable sinter‐resistance and water tolerance. Particularly, after aging at 850 °C, the Pt/HEO catalytic system maintained its full CO conversion for 338 h without any decline. These results highlight the positive effect of increasing configurational entropy on the thermal stability of the entire catalytic system, providing a reliable solution for catalytic conversions involving high temperatures.Keywords: CO oxidation, high‐entropy oxide, nanofibers, Pt, sinter‐resistance The hig

The oxidation of CO, a key reaction in automotive emission abatement, has been extensively investigated in the past decades. Therefore, the light-off curves of CO oxidation are measured to evaluate the catalytic efficiency of our as-obtained samples. As depicted in Fig. 5d, HEFO exhibits an inferior catalytic activity of CO oxidation with a high onset temperature of 230 °C. After doping 1 wt% Pd, Pd1@HEFO shows a dramatically enhanced reactivity with the onset temperature as low as ~80 °C and complete CO oxidation at 170 °C. In comparison, the onset temperature and T100 over Pd@CeO2 are 223 and 253 °C, respectively, much higher than those of Pd1@HEFO. It is generally accepted that metal on reducible carrier (CeO2) follows a Mars–van Krevelen reaction mechanism, where CO adsorbed on metals reacts with active lattice O from CeO2 to form oxygen vacancies,. Therefore, the reducibility of the surface lattice O from the carrier plays an important role in catalytic CO oxidation. For Pd@CeO2, the only reduction peak observed at around 250 °C is assigned to the reduction of Pd–O–Pd (PdOx) and the surface lattice oxygen in CeO2,. papers.title: Sinter- and Water-Resistant Pt Enabled by High Entropy of Porous Oxide Nanofibers.
papers.system: Porous high-entropy oxide (HEO) nanofibers loaded with sub‐2.6 nm Pt nanoparticles
papers.approach: Electrospinning to create porous HEO nanofibers that, via the high‐entropy effect, reduce surface free energy and stabilize Pt nanoparticles against sintering and water-induced degradation
papers.findings: Pt nanoparticles remained nearly unchanged in size (from 2.6 nm to ~2.9–4.2 nm) even after aging at temperatures up to 950 °C and under humid conditions; the catalyst maintained 100% CO conversion over extended testing (338 h and 35-cycle water exposure tests)
papers.mechanism: High configurational mixing entropy lowers the overall Gibbs free energy of the system and reduces the thermodynamic driving force for sintering, while the nanoporous structure further impedes nanoparticle aggregation

papers.title: Improving CO Oxidation Catalysis Over High Entropy Spinels by Increasing Disorder.
papers.system: High entropy spinel oxides (M3O4 type, where M is a mix of first‐row transition metals)
papers.approach: Synthesis of spinel oxide catalysts with increasing numbers of metal components (up to 7-metal) by a solventless thermolysis method to boost configurational disorder
papers.findings: The 7‐metal spinel oxide showed a 63% decrease in the T10 (temperature for 10% CO conversion) and improved long‐term stability with only a 4.7% activity decrease over 14 hours compared to lower entropy variants
papers.mechanism: Higher configurational disorder enhances oxygen vacancy formation and tailors the distribution of metal cations, which improves the oxygen activation via the Mars–van Krevelen mechanism and supports robust catalytic activity

papers.title: Self-regeneration of supported transition metals by a high entropy-driven principle.
papers.system: Supported transition metal catalysts on high entropy cubic oxide (Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox)
papers.approach: Utilization of a high entropy oxide support that facilitates in situ reversible exsolution-dissolution of metallic species under alternating redox environments
papers.findings: Provided ultrahigh thermal stability with negligible growth of metallic nanoparticles during high temperature CO2 hydrogenation (>500 h at 400 °C) and demonstrated self-regenerative behavior
papers.mechanism: The high entropy contributes an entropic driving force that not only suppresses sintering but also enables reversible exsolution and reintegration of active metals, thus maintaining active sites under cycling conditions

papers.title: Stabilization by Configurational Entropy of the Cu(II) Active Site during CO Oxidation on Mg0.2Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2O HEO.
papers.approach: Examination of the stabilization of the Cu(II) redox couple within a high-entropy oxide structure during CO oxidation
papers.findings: The HEO catalyst exhibits low-temperature CO oxidation activity and remains resistant to moisture; it stabilizes the Cu(II)/Cu(I) redox cycle despite all cations being in the same formal oxidation state
papers.mechanism: The configurational entropy of the multicomponent oxide yields a stabilizing contribution to the Gibbs free energy that maintains unusual oxidation states and active sites, thus promoting catalytic performance in moisture-rich environments

papers.title: Designing water resistant high entropy oxide materials.
papers.system: High entropy spinel oxides (e.g., (Ni0.2Mg0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2Co0.2)Cr2O4) used for C3H6 oxidation
papers.approach: Entropy engineering via increasing configurational disorder in spinel oxides to reduce water adsorption and enhance hydrothermal stability
papers.findings: The high entropy oxide maintained excellent water resistance (over 100 h of operation in C3H6 oxidation) compared to binary oxides which deactivated within 20 h
papers.mechanism: Higher configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy and weakens the adsorption energy of H2O, thereby impeding catalyst deactivation via moisture poisoning

papers.title: Entropy-stabilized single-atom Pd catalysts via high-entropy fluorite oxide supports.
papers.system: Single-atom Pd catalysts supported on high entropy fluorite oxide (HEFO)
papers.approach: Doping 1 wt% Pd onto a high entropy fluorite oxide to lower the CO oxidation onset temperature and provide resistance against hydrothermal degradation
papers.findings: Pd1@HEFO showed complete CO oxidation at a notably low temperature (~170 °C) with an onset as low as ~80 °C, outperforming conventional Pd/CeO2 catalysts, and exhibited high stability under oxygen-rich conditions
papers.mechanism: Enhanced reducibility of the surface lattice oxygen near Pd, due to the high entropy support modifying the metal-oxygen interface, facilitates a Mars–van Krevelen reaction mechanism while resisting sintering under hydrothermal conditions

established: High configurational entropy in oxide catalysts lowers the Gibbs free energy, offering improved sinter-resistance and thermal stability.
Increasing the number of constituent metals (i.e., greater disorder) can lower the activation temperatures for CO oxidation and enhance catalyst stability over time.
Porous support structures and high entropy effects can effectively stabilize noble metal nanoparticles at low loadings, maintaining activity in moisture-rich and high-temperature conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Embedding low-loading Pt nanoparticles on high-entropy oxide (HEO) nanofibers
approaches_tried.outcome: Achieved exceptional sinter- and water-resistance with prolonged CO oxidation performance even under high-temperature aging and hydrothermal conditions

approaches_tried.approach: Increasing configurational disorder in spinel oxide catalysts by using multi-metal compositions
approaches_tried.outcome: Significantly reduced low-temperature CO conversion metrics (e.g., 63% reduction in T10) and improved long-term stability under lean, dry conditions

approaches_tried.approach: Utilizing high entropy-driven reversible metal exsolution in oxide supports
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated self-regeneration and sustained catalytic activity over extended high-temperature operation without significant nanoparticle growth

mechanisms: Reduction in surface free energy via high configurational entropy, which suppresses nanoparticle sintering
Enhanced formation and stabilization of oxygen vacancies that drive Mars–van Krevelen oxidation mechanisms
Stabilization of unstable oxidation states (e.g., Cu(II) in a rock-salt structure) via the entropic contribution from multiple metal species
Reversible exsolution-dissolution of metal species enabling self-regeneration under cycling redox conditions
disagreements: While some studies emphasize the role of oxygen vacancy formation in boosting activity, others focus on the purely thermodynamic stabilization of nanoparticle size; the relative contributions of these factors under realistic automotive conditions remain debated.

There is variation in reported optimal compositions. Some works focus on noble-metal assisted catalysts (e.g., Pt/HEO or Pd1@HEFO) while others explore entirely PGM‐free HE oxides, leaving questions about the best balance between PGM use and overall catalytic performance.
open_questions: Can a single intervention be identified that simultaneously enhances low-temperature activity, poisoning resistance, and long-term durability in real-world automotive exhaust conditions?

How do transient operating conditions, such as those encountered during vehicle start-up and variable load, affect the performance of high-entropy catalysts in the presence of typical poisons like water and NO?
What are the long-term degradation pathways under realistic durability tests (including mileage-related issues) for multi-principal-element alloy catalysts and their high entropy oxide supports?
opportunities: Investigate a modification to the near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst by incorporating a high entropy oxide surface layer or coating that can stabilize active sites, impart water and poison resistance, and suppress sintering without increasing PGM loading.
Explore integration of reversible metal exsolution mechanisms into the catalyst design to enable self-regeneration during redox cycling under automotive transient conditions.

Combine the strategies of increasing configurational disorder (as in high entropy spinels) with the stabilization of single-atom noble metal sites (as in Pd1@HEFO) to seamlessly balance high activity with durability and reduced precious metal content.

Conduct in situ studies under realistic exhaust gas compositions (including H2O, NO, and other potential poisons) to fine-tune the catalyst composition and structure for optimal performance over a vehicle lifetime.

directions.direction: Surface-coating modification with a high-entropy oxide (HEO) layer
directions.assessment: Directly alters the catalyst’s outer surface to generate a conformal, nanoporous HEO layer that is known to stabilize active sites against sintering, suppress water and NO poisoning, and promote low-temperature oxidation. The literature (e.g., PMC12224923::web::004::introduction, PMC11436891::web::000::abstract) supports that HEO coatings provide lower Gibbs free energy and robust structural stability. High feasibility using deposition techniques such as ALD or sol–gel makes this a strong candidate.

directions.direction: Induced self‐regeneration through reversible metal exsolution
directions.assessment: By applying a controlled redox thermal cycle to activate reversible exsolution/dissolution, the catalyst can intermittently regenerate active sites. Evidence (PMC8505510::web::000::abstract) shows high-entropy supports enabling in situ self‐regeneration, which addresses long-term durability. However, ensuring uniform cycling under automotive transient conditions is moderately challenging.

directions.direction: Minimal single-atom Pt doping via atomic-layer deposition
directions.assessment: Introducing trace amounts of single-atom Pt (or similar PGM) on the catalyst surface can enhance low-temperature oxidations and improve poison resistance without sacrificing the goal of low PGM use. Studies (e.g., PMC7413391::web::011::catalytic_performance) indicate that isolated noble metal sites are more active and tolerant to contaminants. This intervention directly leverages alloy cohesion while using minimal precious metal.

directions.direction: Nanostructuring to create a controlled nanoporous architecture
directions.assessment: Engineering a nanoporous structure in the multi‐principal‐element alloy can immobilize active sites, improve reactant transport at low temperatures, and mitigate agglomeration/sintering. Although not as directly linked to poison resistance as the HEO coating, literature (PMC12224923::web::019::catalytic_activity_and_stability_assessm) shows porous supports enhance thermal and hydrothermal durability. This is feasible with templated etching or dealloying processes.

candidates.hypothesis: A thin, conformal high-entropy oxide (HEO) coating on the near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst improves low-temperature oxidation activity, resists water and NO poisoning, and enhances lifetime durability without increasing PGM content.
candidates.intervention: Deposit a 2–5 nm thick nanoporous high-entropy oxide layer (e.g., a spinel-type HEO synthesized via a sol–gel or atomic layer deposition method) onto the catalyst surface.

candidates.hypothesis: Thermal pre-treatment cycles that induce controlled, reversible exsolution of metallic clusters from the multi-principal-element alloy provide self-regeneration of active sites, leading to enhanced poisoning resistance and long-term durability.
candidates.intervention: Subject the catalyst to periodic mild redox cycles (e.g., alternating treatments at 400 °C in a reducing atmosphere with 5–10 vol% H2 followed by re-oxidation in air) to trigger in situ reversible exsolution of finely dispersed metal clusters.

candidates.hypothesis: Introducing trace single-atom Pt via atomic layer deposition onto the catalyst surface will create isolated noble metal sites that enhance low-temperature CO/hydrocarbon oxidation and improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning without significantly increasing overall PGM usage.
candidates.intervention: Utilize atomic layer deposition to deposit approximately 1 wt% (or lower) of Pt as isolated single atoms dispersed across the catalyst surface.

candidates.hypothesis: Engineering a controlled nanoporous architecture on the surface of the multi-principal-element alloy catalyst enhances reactant accessibility and immobilizes active sites, thereby improving low-temperature oxidation kinetics, poison resistance, and long-term durability.
candidates.intervention: Apply a controlled etching or templating process (e.g., using selective chemical etchants or removable pore formers) to generate an interconnected nanoporous structure (with pore sizes in the 5–20 nm range) on the catalyst surface.

minor_issues: Long-term chemical compatibility and adhesion of the high-entropy oxide coating on the base alloy are not fully clarified.
Exact preparation conditions (e.g., sol–gel vs. ALD) and process reproducibility require more detail.
fixes: Include data on coating integrity after extended thermal cycling, with explicit characterization (e.g., cross-sectional TEM, XPS) to confirm that the HEO layer remains stable and well-adhered.
Quantify the effect of the coating thickness and stoichiometry on catalytic activity, poison tolerance, and sintering resistance.
evidence_needs: Empirical accelerated aging study of the full coated system in automotive-like conditions (thermal, mechanical, chemical) to confirm retention of activity and structure.
Experimental or computational data on the HEO–metal interface (e.g., interdiffusion kinetics, phase stability) to ensure the claimed sinter- and poison-resistance is maintained.

minor_issues: Practicality of performing repeated mild redox cycles during real driving conditions needs clarification.
The proportion of alloy elements capable of forming stable oxide phases that can exsolve metal clusters is not fully discussed.
fixes: Demonstrate that the exsolution-based approach can be integrated with standard automotive engine management strategy (e.g., cold start, partial load cycles).
Clarify the fraction of exsolvable phases within the multi-principal-element alloy and how exsolution reacts to typical automotive temperature ramps.
evidence_needs: Detailed microstructural study (e.g., in situ STEM or XRD) during repeated redox cycles under realistic auto-exhaust conditions to confirm stable, reversible exsolution behavior.
Comparison with a well-known exsolution-based system (e.g., perovskite or spinel) operated in an automotive test bench to benchmark achievable self-regeneration.

minor_issues: Ensuring single-atom Pt remains atomically dispersed under prolonged high-temperature and redox cycling is uncertain.
Long-term sintering or clustering of Pt could occur and diminish the intended performance gain.
fixes: Incorporate advanced support interactions (e.g., doping the support or controlling surface ligands) to stabilize single-atom Pt under severe aging conditions.
Optimize the Pt loading to confirm minimal PGM usage for maximum performance returns.
evidence_needs: Extended (≥500 h) on-engine or test-bench aging data demonstrating stable single-atom dispersion and sustained low-temperature activity.
Comparative tests with different Pt loadings to identify thresholds where performance is significantly improved without substantial PGM cost.

minor_issues: The manufacturing feasibility and scale-up of controlled nanoporous structures on an automotive catalyst are not discussed.
Stability of the nanoscale porosity under high-temperature and vibrational conditions typical of vehicle operation remains unproven.
fixes: Conduct systematic studies on pore-size tuning, control of pore connectivity, and the resulting effects on catalytic performance under realistic automotive cycles.
Provide mechanical integrity and thermal stability data for the porous layer after repeated thermal shocks and vibrations.
evidence_needs: Accelerated aging experiments (thermal, mechanical) coupled with in situ characterization (e.g., X-ray tomography) to confirm that the porous structure persists.
Comparative data showing that the nanoporous layer indeed lowers the light-off temperature and improves tolerance to NO/H2O versus identical catalyst compositions without porosity.
